Option (d) — Great Himalayan National Park designated UNESCO Natural WHS in 2014 is correct.
Option (c) is NOT correctly matched — option (c) is the answer.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap replaces 2011 (the correct year Manas was removed from the 'In Danger' list) with 2008. Students who know Manas was on the danger list and was removed will accept the pairing as broadly correct without scrutinising the specific year. The 2011 removal year is a precision-tested fact. Selecting option (b) (Western Ghats 2012) as the incorrect pair is the counter-trap for students who recall the WHS year approximately.
solution.final_explanation:
India's UNESCO Natural World Heritage Sites have distinct histories, including the case of Manas WHS which faced an extraordinary conservation trajectory.

• Option (a) — Correctly matched: Sundarbans is indeed both a UNESCO Natural WHS (1987) and a Ramsar Site — part of its 'quintuple designation.'
• Option (b) — Correctly matched: Western Ghats was designated a UNESCO Natural WHS in 2012, spanning six states.
• Option (c) — NOT correctly matched: Manas WHS was removed from the UNESCO 'In Danger' list in 2011, not 2008. This is the incorrect pair.
• Option (d) — Correctly matched: Great Himalayan National Park was designated a UNESCO Natural WHS in 2014.

Value Addition:
• Manas was placed on the In Danger list in 1992 due to civil conflict and poaching; it was removed in 2011 after significant recovery.
• The 'In Danger' listing triggers enhanced international monitoring but does not remove WHS status.
• Nanda Devi and Valley of Flowers NP cluster (Uttarakhand) was designated WHS in 1988, making it one of India's earlier natural heritage sites.

solution.concept_anchor: Corridors no statutory protection; grasslands underrepresented in PA network

statement_analysis.statement: Wildlife corridors identified in conservation management plans in India are legally enforceable under the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972, which grants them Right of Way through private and revenue land.
statement_analysis.reason: Wildlife corridors have no statutory protection under WPA 1972; they appear in management plans as conservation tools but cannot be legally enforced as WPA provisions.

statement_analysis.statement: Shola forests of the Western Ghats are unique montane ecosystems that are under-threat from invasive Eucalyptus and Wattle plantations, even within Protected Area boundaries.
statement_analysis.reason: Shola forests are threatened by Eucalyptus and Wattle plantations within and around PAs like Eravikulam NP; this is a documented conservation challenge, making this statement correct.

statement_analysis.statement: India's National Biodiversity Action Plan and the UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration (2021–2030) are both aligned in calling for active restoration of degraded ecosystems including grasslands and mangroves.
statement_analysis.reason: Both NBAP and the UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration (2021–2030) specifically call for ecosystem restoration including grasslands and mangroves; this statement is correct.

solution.strong_distractor: c — 'Statements 2 and 3' appears to be the answer but students selecting it have confused the structure — the question asks for NOT correct, so they should pick Statement 1 only.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 — corridors lack statutory enforcement under WPA 1972; 'Right of Way through private land' is not a WPA provision — Statement 1 is NOT correct, making it the answer.
Statement 2 — Shola forest Eucalyptus/Wattle threat within PAs is factually documented — Statement 2 IS correct, so not the answer.
Statement 3 — NBAP and UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration both call for ecosystem restoration — Statement 3 IS correct, so not the answer.
Only Statement 1 is NOT correct — option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in Statement 1 adds 'legally enforceable' and 'Right of Way through private and revenue land' to wildlife corridors — both are fabrications. Corridors are real conservation tools but have no WPA legal backing. Students who know corridors are important may accept Statement 1 as broadly describing what corridors should have, confusing aspirational policy language with current legal status.
solution.final_explanation:
Landscape-level conservation requires attention to both corridors connecting PAs and the health of ecosystems within PA boundaries.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect (the answer): Wildlife corridors in India have no statutory backing under WPA 1972. They are identified in management plans and conservation strategies, but the 'Right of Way' concept is an administrative aspiration, not an enforceable legal provision.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Shola forests in the Western Ghats (protected within NPs like Eravikulam) are genuinely threatened by invasive Eucalyptus and Silver Wattle plantations, including within PA boundaries — a documented afforestation-vs-restoration conflict.
• Statement 3 — Correct: India's National Biodiversity Action Plan and the global UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration (2021–2030) both emphasise active restoration of degraded ecosystems including grasslands, mangroves, and forests.

Value Addition:
• The Kaziranga–Karbi Anglong corridor (National Highway 37 conflict) is the most cited example of corridor protection challenges.
• Restoration vs. afforestation: planting monoculture trees in shola grassland patches is counterproductive and worsens biodiversity loss.
• Project Elephant's 'Gajah' report is the primary document identifying India's elephant corridors.

solution.concept_anchor: WPA 1972 — key amendments timeline: 2002, 2006, 2022
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) places the 2006 (Tiger Reserves/NTCA) amendment before the 2002 (Community Reserves/Conservation Reserves) amendment, which students who confuse amendment years will select.
elimination_logic: Original WPA enacted in 1972 — this is always the first event.
2002 WPA Amendment introduced Community Reserves and Conservation Reserves — this is the second dated event.
2006 WPA Amendment inserted Section 38V (Tiger Reserves) and created NTCA — this follows 2002.
2022 WPA Amendment reduced schedules from 6 to 4 and removed vermin provisions — most recent; correct order is I → III → II → IV, option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap reverses the 2002 and 2006 amendments, which many students conflate. Students who know both amendments introduced significant changes may not remember which came first. Option (c) reverses them, catching students who recall both but are uncertain about the sequence. The 2022 amendment is the easiest to place last; the trap is in ordering 2002 vs. 2006.
solution.final_explanation:
The Wildlife Protection Act 1972 has undergone several significant amendments since its original enactment, each introducing distinct conservation mechanisms.

I — Enactment of Wildlife Protection Act (1972): established the original framework including Schedule I–VI species protection, NP and WLS categories.
II — 2006 WPA Amendment: inserted Section 38V creating Tiger Reserves and Section 38L establishing NTCA.
III — 2002 WPA Amendment: introduced Conservation Reserves (Section 36A) and Community Reserves (Section 36C) as new PA categories.
IV — 2022 WPA Amendment: restructured schedules from 6 to 4, removed vermin provisions, aligned with CITES obligations.

Correct chronological order: I (1972) → III (2002) → II (2006) → IV (2022) — option (a).

Value Addition:
• The 2002 amendment's Community Reserves were partly inspired by joint forest management experiences.
• Section 38V (2006) made NTCA a statutory body with supervisory powers over Tiger Reserves.
• The 2022 amendment updated species lists to align with CITES Appendix listings, an important India-international obligation link.

statement_analysis.statement: The Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) Notification issued under the Environment Protection Act, 1986 constitutes the primary instrument for declaring and managing Marine Protected Areas in India.
statement_analysis.reason: CRZ Notification regulates coastal land use and construction activities; it is a separate instrument from Marine PA declarations, which are made under WPA 1972. India lacks a dedicated MPA law.

statement_analysis.statement: Eco-Sensitive Zones around National Parks and Wildlife Sanctuaries derive their legal authority from the Environment Protection Act, 1986, not from the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972.
statement_analysis.reason: ESZs are notified under EPA 1986; they are not a WPA 1972 mechanism — this is the definitive legal position.

statement_analysis.statement: India's Marine National Parks and Marine Wildlife Sanctuaries are currently governed under the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972.
statement_analysis.reason: Marine NPs (like Gulf of Kutch) and Marine WLS are declared under WPA 1972 in the same manner as terrestrial PAs; WPA applies to both terrestrial and marine categories.

statement_analysis.statement: Activities such as commercial mining and setting up of hotels are both categorised as 'prohibited activities' within Eco-Sensitive Zones under the Environment Protection Act, 1986.
statement_analysis.reason: Commercial mining is prohibited in ESZs, but hotels and resorts may be permitted with regulation; they are not in the prohibited category — they fall under regulated activities depending on size and location.

solution.strong_distractor: c — 'Only three' tempts students who correctly identify Statement 1 as wrong but do not check Statement 4, accepting hotels as prohibited alongside mining.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 — CRZ is NOT the instrument for declaring MPAs; WPA 1972 governs marine NPs and WLS; Statement 1 is incorrect.
Statement 2 — ESZs are under EPA 1986 not WPA 1972; Statement 2 is correct.
Statement 3 — Marine NPs and WLS are under WPA 1972; Statement 3 is correct.
Statement 4 — commercial mining is prohibited in ESZs, but hotels/resorts are regulated (not categorically prohibited); Statement 4 is incorrect.
Two statements correct (2 and 3) — option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 4 uses conflation — merging 'commercial mining' (prohibited) with hotels/resorts (regulated) into a single 'prohibited' category. Students who know mining is prohibited in ESZs may extend this prohibition to all commercial activities including hotels without checking the regulatory differentiation. Statement 1 conflates CRZ (coastal land-use regulation) with MPA declaration — a classic instrument-swap.
solution.final_explanation:
India's coastal and marine conservation operates through multiple legal instruments that must be distinguished precisely.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: CRZ Notification (EPA 1986) is a land-use regulation for coastal zones; it does NOT constitute the instrument for declaring MPAs. Marine NPs and WLS are declared under WPA 1972.
• Statement 2 — Correct: ESZs are notified under EPA 1986, not WPA 1972 — a core fact for UPSC.
• Statement 3 — Correct: India's Marine National Parks and Marine WLS (Gulf of Kutch, Mahatma Gandhi Marine NP) are governed under WPA 1972.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: In ESZs, commercial mining is prohibited, but hotels, resorts, and similar establishments are placed in the 'regulated activities' category, not the prohibited list. Hotels may be permitted subject to conditions.

Only Statements 2 and 3 are correct — option (b).

Value Addition:
• ESZ regulated activities include felling of trees and establishment of industries; permitted activities include ongoing agriculture.
• The absence of a dedicated MPA law means India's marine biodiversity governance has significant jurisdictional and enforcement gaps.
• CRZ-I areas include ecologically sensitive areas like mangroves, coral reefs, and sand dunes — these receive the highest CRZ protection.

solution.concept_anchor: Biosphere Reserve zones — Transition allows settlements; Core strictly protected

statement_analysis.statement: In the three-zone model of a UNESCO-MAB Biosphere Reserve, the Transition (Cooperation) Zone is the outermost zone where human settlements and sustainable use activities are permitted.
statement_analysis.reason: The Transition/Cooperation Zone is the outermost zone of BRs where human habitation and sustainable economic activities are permitted — this is correct per UNESCO-MAB framework.

statement_analysis.statement: The Core Zone of a Biosphere Reserve in India has the same legal status as a National Park declared under Section 35 of the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972.
statement_analysis.reason: Biosphere Reserves have no statutory backing under Indian law; the Core Zone is administratively protected but does NOT have the same statutory status as a National Park under WPA 1972 — even if an NP exists within the BR core zone, the BR designation itself carries no statutory weight.

statement_analysis.statement: India's Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve, the first BR established in the country (1986), encompasses multiple National Parks and Wildlife Sanctuaries within its area, illustrating the overlap between BR and statutory PA designations.
statement_analysis.reason: Nilgiri BR (1986) is the first and largest BR in India; it covers parts of Tamil Nadu, Kerala, and Karnataka and contains Mudumalai WLS, Nagarhole NP, Bandipur NP, Silent Valley NP, and others.

solution.strong_distractor: d — 'All three' is the distractor for students who assume the Core Zone of a BR must have legal status equivalent to an NP since NPs often sit within BR cores.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 — Transition Zone is outermost, allows human settlements in UNESCO-MAB framework — correct.

Statement 2 — Core Zone of a BR does NOT have statutory NP status under WPA; BRs have no statutory backing; even if an NP lies within the core, the BR's Core Zone designation by itself is non-statutory — Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 3 — Nilgiri BR (1986) is first, largest, contains multiple NPs and WLS — correct.
Only Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the common overlap between BR Core Zones and NPs/WLS. Students see that many BR Core Zones contain NPs and assume the Core Zone therefore has NP-level statutory protection. The trap is that the BR designation itself has no statutory weight — it is the NP or WLS within the core that provides legal protection, not the BR label. The Core Zone of a BR without an underlying NP/WLS has no comparable statutory standing.
solution.final_explanation:
The UNESCO-MAB Biosphere Reserve framework prescribes a three-zone model as an international management standard, but India's BRs lack a domestic statutory foundation.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Transition (Cooperation) Zone is the outermost layer of the BR three-zone model; it permits human settlements and sustainable economic activities — this is the correct UNESCO-MAB characterisation.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Core Zone of a BR does NOT automatically have NP-equivalent statutory status. Biosphere Reserves are executive notifications without legislative backing. If an NP exists within the core, the NP's WPA status provides legal protection — not the BR designation itself.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Nilgiri BR (1986) is India's first Biosphere Reserve. It spans Tamil Nadu, Kerala, and Karnataka and overlaps with multiple NPs (Bandipur, Nagarhole, Mudumalai, Silent Valley) and WLS — a model example of PA-BR overlap.

Value Addition:
• Buffer Zone of a BR permits limited research, eco-tourism, and traditional use activities.
• BR overlap with NPs/WLS is administratively convenient but creates dual management authority questions.
• 12 of India's 18 BRs are UNESCO-MAB recognised; Cold Desert and Dibru-Saikhowa are notable non-UNESCO BRs.

solution.concept_anchor: Conservation success paradox — rising populations increase HWC
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) tempts students who accept both as true and assume the causal direction 'rising populations → more conflict' is precisely what R is saying.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. Retaliatory killings and poaching driven by conflict are documented consequences of increased HWC, which itself is linked to conservation success in expanding populations.
Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. Conservation success — growing tiger and elephant populations — is indeed a documented driver of increased HWC as animals range into human-dominated landscapes.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — No. R explains why HWC is increasing, not why HWC leads to retaliatory killing and poaching. The causal mechanism linking HWC to poaching (A) is community resentment and economic loss — R merely explains why HWC itself is rising, not why it causes the specific conservation threat of poaching/retaliatory killing.
Both A and R are correct, but R does not explain A — option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The reversed-causation trap here is subtle. R correctly states that rising wildlife populations increase HWC. A correctly states that HWC drives retaliatory killings and poaching. A student will read them together and see a logical chain: more animals → more conflict → more poaching. But R does not explain WHY HWC leads to retaliatory killing — it only explains why HWC is increasing. The causal link in A (HWC causing retaliatory killing) depends on community resentment and economic loss, not on population size alone. R and A describe sequential events, not a causal explanation.
solution.final_explanation:
Human-Wildlife Conflict represents one of conservation's most complex paradoxes: the very success of conservation programmes creates new threats.

• Assertion (A): Correct. Rising HWC incidents — crop raids, livestock predation, and occasional human casualties — generate community resentment that manifests as retaliatory killings and sympathy for poachers. HWC is a genuine driver of poaching pressure.
• Reason (R): Correct. India's conservation successes (Project Tiger, Project Elephant) have led to genuine population recovery — tiger numbers have grown, elephant ranges have expanded — increasing the frequency of encounters with human settlements.
• Causal link: Absent (in the precise explanatory sense). R explains why HWC is increasing (more animals, expanded ranges), but it does not explain why HWC leads specifically to retaliatory killing and poaching (A). That mechanism involves community economics, inadequate compensation, and anger — not covered by R.

Both A and R are correct but R does NOT explain A — option (b).

Value Addition:
• India has no national mandatory HWC compensation law; state ex-gratia schemes are inconsistent.
• The 2022 removal of the vermin provision limits states' ability to manage conflict species through culling.
• Eco-tourism revenue from tiger reserves is cited as a 'conservation pays' counterargument to HWC-driven community opposition.

solution.concept_anchor: OECMs — Other Effective Area-Based Conservation Measures under Kunming-Montreal
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is the strong distractor because students who know India's PA coverage is ~5% assume the only path to 30x30 is expanding traditional PAs, missing the OECM concept.
elimination_logic: The scenario describes protected forests, sacred groves, and community-managed lands outside formal PA boundaries contributing to 30x30 — this describes OECMs.
Eliminate option (a) — converting all such areas into NPs/WLS is neither practical nor legally required; 30x30 explicitly allows non-traditional conservation areas.
Eliminate option (b) — Community Reserves exist only on community/private land declared under WPA; the scenario includes diverse land categories beyond this specific legal category.
Eliminate option (d) — the 30x30 target explicitly includes areas outside formal PA boundaries through OECMs; option (d) incorrectly states only formal PAs count.
Option (c) correctly identifies OECMs (Other Effective Area-Based Conservation Measures) as the mechanism by which non-formal conservation areas count towards the 30x30 target.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in option (d) limits '30x30 counting' to only formally declared PAs — incorrect. The Kunming-Montreal GBF explicitly introduced OECMs as a mechanism for countries to account for conservation areas outside formal PA boundaries. This includes indigenous community lands, sacred groves, private conservation areas, and sustainably managed forests. Students who think of conservation in terms of formal NP/WLS/Tiger Reserve categories will miss the OECM dimension.
solution.final_explanation:
The Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework's '30x30' target — protecting 30% of land and ocean by 2030 — introduced a critical new concept: Other Effective Area-Based Conservation Measures (OECMs). These allow countries to count conservation areas outside formally declared PAs toward the 30% target.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Converting all such areas into NPs or Tiger Reserves is not required by 30x30; OECMs allow recognition of diverse governance arrangements without requiring formal PA declaration.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Community Reserves are a specific WPA 1972 category declared on community/private land; the scenario encompasses a much wider range of land types beyond this specific category.
• Option (c) — Correct: Sacred groves, sustainably managed community forests, and protected areas outside formal PA boundaries can qualify as OECMs under the Kunming-Montreal GBF, allowing them to count towards the 30x30 commitment.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The 30x30 framework explicitly recognises OECMs and does not restrict counting to formally declared NPs, WLS, or Tiger Reserves alone.

Value Addition:
• India's PA network currently covers ~5% of geographic area; meeting 30x30 requires massive OECM recognition.
• Sacred groves (devvans/devkots) in India represent traditional community conservation and are strong OECM candidates.
• OECMs were a key negotiating outcome of CBD COP 15 (Kunming-Montreal, December 2022).

statement_analysis.statement: Among all categories of Protected Areas in India, only Biosphere Reserves are declared by the Central Government; National Parks, Wildlife Sanctuaries, Conservation Reserves, and Community Reserves are all declared by State Governments under the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972.
statement_analysis.reason: This correctly identifies the Central Government's role for BRs and State Government's role for all WPA-governed categories (NPs, WLS, Conservation Reserves, Community Reserves).

statement_analysis.statement: The National Board for Wildlife can directly order the de-notification of a National Park if it determines that the area is required for a project of national importance.
statement_analysis.reason: NBWL is an advisory body; it cannot order de-notification. De-notification of an NP also requires Supreme Court approval and NBWL alone cannot authorise it regardless of the project's importance.

statement_analysis.statement: In a Wildlife Sanctuary, the Collector (or designated officer) may settle rights of persons under the provisions of the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972, but no such settlement of rights is permissible within a National Park after its declaration.
statement_analysis.reason: WPA 1972 allows settlement of rights in WLS through the Collector; after an NP is declared, no settlement of rights is permissible — this is the precise legal distinction.

solution.strong_distractor: d — 'All three' is the distractor for students who don't check whether NBWL has direct de-notification power or confuse its advisory role with executive authority.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 — Central Govt declares BRs; State Govts declare all WPA categories; this is correct.
Statement 2 — NBWL cannot 'directly order' de-notification; it is advisory; de-notification additionally requires Supreme Court approval; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 3 — Collector settles rights in WLS; no settlement permissible in NP after declaration — this is the precise WPA position; Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct — option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 uses partial-truth: NBWL is involved in de-notification processes (it recommends), but stating it can 'directly order' de-notification overstates its authority. NBWL is advisory, and de-notification of an NP additionally requires Supreme Court approval. The phrase 'project of national importance' sounds like it might create an exception, further tempting students who believe urgent national projects override conservation procedures.
solution.final_explanation:
This question integrates three key dimensions of India's PA governance: the declaring authority distinction, NBWL's advisory limits, and the settlement-of-rights distinction between NPs and WLS.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Biosphere Reserves are declared by the Central Government (MoEFCC executive notification); all categories under WPA 1972 (NP, WLS, Conservation Reserve, Community Reserve) are declared by State Governments.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: NBWL is constituted under Section 5A of WPA 1972 as an advisory body. It cannot directly order de-notification; it can only recommend. De-notification of an NP additionally requires Supreme Court approval — no project-based exception overrides this.
• Statement 3 — Correct: WPA 1972 permits the Collector to settle rights of local persons within a WLS through a defined process; after an NP is declared, the Act explicitly prohibits any settlement of rights — this is the sharpest legal distinction between the two categories.

Value Addition:
• The Collector's role in WLS rights settlement is akin to a revenue/judicial process — claims are examined and settled or rejected with compensation.
• Section 35(8) of WPA: after NP declaration, no rights can be acquired within the NP without government permission.
• NBWL Standing Committee meetings are far more frequent than full NBWL meetings; project clearances happen at the Standing Committee level.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is the strong distractor; Keoladeo Ghana NP is both a Ramsar site and a UNESCO Natural WHS, but students may not remember it was also on the Montreux Record and doubt the pairing.
elimination_logic: Option (a) — Keoladeo Ghana NP is both a Ramsar site and a UNESCO Natural WHS; this pairing is correct.
Option (b) — Loktak Lake (Manipur) remains on the Montreux Record; this pairing is correct.
Option (c) — Sundarbans is simultaneously a Biosphere Reserve, NP, Tiger Reserve, Ramsar Site, and UNESCO Natural WHS — all five; this pairing is correct.

Option (d) — Gulf of Mannar is a Marine Biosphere Reserve (India's first marine BR, 1989), not the Mahatma Gandhi Marine NP; the Mahatma Gandhi Marine NP is in the Andaman & Nicobar Islands; pairing 'Gulf of Mannar' with 'first Marine NP in India' is incorrect because Gulf of Mannar Marine NP (if that is implied) is not the same as the Mahatma Gandhi Marine NP — more precisely, Gulf of Mannar Biosphere Reserve was India's first marine BR, but the Gulf of Kutch Marine NP is the relevant marine NP frequently cited; option (d) incorrectly identifies the Gulf of Mannar Biosphere Reserve as the first Marine National Park — it is a Biosphere Reserve, not an NP.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The geographic-swap trap in option (d) assigns 'first Marine National Park in India' to the Gulf of Mannar, which is actually India's first Marine Biosphere Reserve (1989). The first Marine National Park in India is the Gulf of Kutch Marine NP (Gujarat), not the Gulf of Mannar. Students who know Gulf of Mannar is significant for marine conservation but have not precisely distinguished its BR status from NP status will accept the pairing. The Mahatma Gandhi Marine NP (Andaman & Nicobar) is the other notable marine NP.
solution.final_explanation:
International conservation designations for India's wetlands and coastal areas require careful distinction.

• Option (a) — Correctly matched: Keoladeo Ghana NP (Rajasthan) is a Ramsar site and a UNESCO Natural WHS (1985); it was also on the Montreux Record before being removed.
• Option (b) — Correctly matched: Loktak Lake (Manipur) remains on the Ramsar Montreux Record due to hydrological alterations from the Loktak Hydroelectric Project.
• Option (c) — Correctly matched: Sundarbans holds all five designations — NP, Tiger Reserve, Biosphere Reserve, UNESCO Natural WHS, and Ramsar Site — the 'quintuple designation.'
• Option (d) — NOT correctly matched: The Gulf of Mannar is India's first Marine Biosphere Reserve (1989), not a Marine National Park. India's notable Marine National Parks are the Gulf of Kutch Marine NP (Gujarat) and the Mahatma Gandhi Marine NP (Andaman & Nicobar Islands).

Value Addition:
• Gulf of Mannar BR spans Tamil Nadu coast and includes 21 islands with coral reefs.
• Gulf of Kutch Marine NP was established in 1982 — one of the earliest marine PAs in India.
• Montreux Record inclusion signals international concern but does not trigger automatic removal from Ramsar status.
